chunks: Muhammad ibn Ibrahim narrated, saying: Abu al-Qasim Uthman ibn Hammad narrated, saying: Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Daqqaq narrated, saying: Ishaq ibn Wahb al-Affaf narrated, saying: Mansur ibn al-Muhajir narrated, saying: Muhammad ibn Ata narrated from Aisha, that a young man was a companion of listening (to sermons/events), and whenever the crescent of Dhu al-Hijjah appeared, he would become a fasting person in the morning. The news rose to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), so he sent for him and called him, saying: 'What compels you to fast these days?'
'May my father and mother be sacrificed for you, O Messenger of Allah, these are the days of Mashar and the days of Hajj; it is hoped that Allah will include me in their prayers.'

'For you, for every day you fast, is the reward equal to freeing a slave, sacrificing one hundred camels, and carrying a load on one hundred horses in the way of Allah, and expiation for sixty years before it and sixty years after it.'

key_terms.ذِي الْحِجَّةِ: Dhu al-Hijjah (the 12th month of the Islamic calendar)

ai.seo_question: What is the reward for fasting during the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah according to this hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Thawab al-Amal*, the Prophet (peace be upon him) highlights the spiritual synergy between fasting and the pilgrims' supplications during the first nine days of Dhu al-Hijjah, a period known as the 'Days of Mashar'. The immense reward—equivalent to freeing a slave, sacrificing a hundred camels, and expiating sixty years of sins—underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on voluntary fasting as a means of spiritual purification and alignment with the sacred rituals of Hajj.
